I farm here in the North East, in the Sudan Savanna where rain comes only from June to September, so I must plan my sorghum carefully. I own this land and I intercrop my sorghum with cowpea as we always do, to spread the risk and feed the soil. I will buy a little NPK and top-dress with urea if the subsidy reaches our area, but fertilizer is costly so I cannot apply a full rate — I will stretch what I can afford. I keep my own sorghum seed from last harvest because the local variety handles our dry spells better than the improved ones I have tried before, and I have no money for pesticides or a pump for irrigation.
